citations.text: Barzilai, S., & Chinn, C. A. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR frameworks of epistemic performance and growth: Reflections on educational theory development. Educational Psychology Review, 36(3), 91.

en.general: A standard or criterion used to judge whether an epistemic aim has been reached and how good the result is. Examples for models are 'supported by evidence', 'not contradicted by any evidence', 'as simple as possible' and 'easily understandable'. Scientists use ideals such as empirical adequacy and fruitfulness.

examples: A class agrees that a good model must fit the evidence it was built from and must not be contradicted by new evidence.
A student rejects a source because the author has a stake in the outcome.
nonExamples: A personal preference for a model because it looks appealing, when the preference plays no role in judging whether the aim was met.
